procedural_history.originating_court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (implied, based on the nature of the case)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 05.01.2017 of the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jodhpur in S. B. Civil Miscellaneous Appeal No. 290 of 2001 connected with S. B. Civil Miscellaneous Appeal No.273 of 2001
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court set aside the Tribunal's award (which presumably favored the appellant) and allowed the appeal filed by the driver and owner of the jeep (respondent Nos. 2 and 3), while dismissing the appeal filed by the appellant. The High Court's decision was based on the investigation report of the jeep, which contradicted the appellant's claim that the jeep had hit his motorcycle.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, dissatisfied with the High Court's decision, appealed to the Supreme Court.

directions: The appeals are allowed in the above terms with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether Jeep No.RST-4701 was involved in the accident and driven rashly and negligently by respondent No.2.

facts: The Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal initially found that Jeep No.RST-4701 was involved in the accident and was driven negligently by respondent No. 2.
The Tribunal based its conclusion on police records, including the FIR, charge-sheet, and Jeep Seizure Report, even though it had some doubts about the oral testimony of certain witnesses.
The High Court reversed the Tribunal's decision. It reasoned that the Tribunal should not have relied on police documents after discarding the oral evidence.
The High Court was also influenced by a Mechanical Investigation Report which noted only a minor scratch on the jeep's mudguard, suggesting it was not involved in a significant accident.
The High Court also stated that the Tribunal had failed to make a specific finding on the driver's negligence.
law: In motor accident claims, the standard of proof required to establish negligence is the 'preponderance of probability,' not the stricter criminal standard of 'proof beyond a reasonable doubt'.
The filing of a police charge-sheet against a driver is considered prima facie evidence pointing towards their complicity and negligent driving in a motor accident claim.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a "manifest error" by overturning the Tribunal's decision.

It held that the Tribunal was correct to take a "holistic view" of all the evidence, including the FIR and charge-sheet, which confirmed the accident and the involvement of the specific jeep and driver.

The Court dismissed the High Court's reliance on the Mechanical Investigation Report (showing only a scratch), noting that the vehicle was seized a month after the accident, and the possibility of it having been repaired could not be ruled out. The High Court's conclusion on this point was deemed to be based on "surmises and conjectures."

The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's assertion that the Tribunal made no finding on negligence. It stated that a finding of rash and negligent driving could be clearly discerned from the Tribunal's reliance on witness evidence and the police charge-sheet naming respondent No. 2.
Applying the standard of 'preponderance of probability,' the Court found that the police records and other evidence were sufficient to establish the jeep's involvement and the driver's negligence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, concluding that the High Court was wrong to reverse the Tribunal's findings. It restored the Tribunal's decision, holding that based on a holistic view of the evidence, particularly the police charge-sheet and other documents, it was established by a preponderance of probability that Jeep No.RST-4701 was involved in the accident and was driven rashly and negligently by respondent No. 2.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Jeep No.RST-4701 was involved in the accident and driven rashly and negligently by respondent No.2.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (claimant) argued that the High Court committed a manifest error in taking a contrary view on the involvement of the jeep and the negligence of its driver.

The appellant contended that the evidence of witnesses PW-1, PW-2, and PW-4, which established the involvement of the offending vehicle and its rash and negligent driving by respondent No.2, should not have been discarded.
respondent_arguments: Respondent Nos. 2 (the driver) and 3 denied that the accident occurred and that the jeep in question was involved.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate court commits a manifest error apparent on the face of the record when it takes a contrary view to a tribunal's finding of fact regarding negligence, especially when the tribunal's finding was based on a consideration of the entirety of the pleadings, evidence, and circumstances.
obiter: The rule of statutory authority will be excluded either when an act was done under a statutory duty or when a statute provides otherwise.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Considering the entirety of the pleadings, evidence and circumstances on record and in particular the finding recorded by the Tribunal on the factum of negligence of the respondent No.2, the driver of the offending jeep, the High Court committed manifest error in taking a contrary view which, in the Court's opinion, is an error apparent on the face of record and manifestly wrong.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the lower court (High Court) committed a 'manifest error' or an 'error apparent on the face of record' when overturning the factual findings of the original fact-finding body (the Tribunal).
